title: Angle Position and Arc Length
learningObjective: Identify and find coterminal angles. Find the length of a circular arc.

faqs.question: What are coterminal angles?
faqs.answer:
Coterminal angles are two (or more) angles that end up with the exact same terminal side when drawn in standard position — even though they represent different amounts of rotation. You can always find another angle coterminal to a given one by adding or subtracting a full 360° rotation, since spinning all the way around a circle brings you right back to where you started.

60° and 420° land on the exact same terminal side — they're coterminal.

faqs.question: What is the principal angle, and why do we usually work with it?
faqs.answer: Since any angle has infinitely many coterminal angles, it's convenient to agree on one "default" representative to work with. The principal angle is that representative — the unique coterminal angle α satisfying 0° ≤ α < 360° (or 0 ≤ α < 2π in radians). Whenever you're handed a large or negative angle, converting it to its principal angle first makes it much easier to visualize and work with.

faqs.question: What is arc length, and how is it different from the angle measure itself?
faqs.answer:
Arc length is the actual DISTANCE traveled along the curved edge of a circle for a given central angle — it's measured in units of length (inches, meters, etc.), not in degrees or radians. The angle measure tells you how much rotation happened; the arc length tells you how far you'd have to physically walk along the circle's edge to match that rotation. The two are related, but they're not the same kind of quantity — one's a rotation, the other's a distance.

The orange curve is the arc — the actual distance along the circle's edge for this 120° angle.

faqs.question: Why does the arc length formula simplify to s = rθ when θ is in radians?
faqs.answer: This connects directly back to TR1's definition of a radian. Remember, 1 radian is defined as the angle that creates an arc exactly as long as the radius — so an angle of θ radians, by that same logic, creates an arc that's θ times the radius long. That's exactly the formula s = rθ; it's not a coincidence, it's the radian definition working exactly as designed. This is also exactly why radians are so useful in more advanced math — the relationship between angle and distance is as simple as it can possibly be.

faqs.question: What is a sector of a circle, and how do I find its area?
faqs.answer:
A sector is the pie-slice-shaped region bounded by two radii and the arc between them. Since a sector is just some fraction of the entire circle, its area is that same fraction of the entire circle's area (πr²) — the fraction being determined by how much of a full rotation (360° or 2π) the central angle represents.

The shaded sector is bounded by two radii and the arc between them.

faqs.question: How do I find angles that are coterminal to a given angle?
faqs.answer:
Add or subtract any whole-number multiple of 360° (or 2π if working in radians). The formula is θ + k·360°, where k can be any integer — positive k gives you larger coterminal angles, negative k gives you smaller (or negative) ones.
Worked Example

Find two angles coterminal to \( 60° \).

Larger: \( 60°+360°=420° \)

Smaller: \( 60°-360°=-300° \)

faqs.question: How do I find the principal angle for an angle that's very large or negative?
faqs.answer:
Repeatedly add or subtract 360° until the result lands between 0° and 360°. For a large positive angle, keep subtracting 360°; for a negative angle, keep adding 360°. If you'd rather skip the repetition, divide the angle by 360° and use just the remainder (adding 360° once more if that remainder comes out negative).
Worked Example

Find the principal angle of \( 830° \).

\( 830° - 360° = 470° \) (still too big)

\( 470° - 360° = 110° \)    (this is between 0° and 360°)

Principal angle: \( 110° \)

faqs.question: How do I find arc length when the angle is given in degrees?
faqs.answer:
Use the formula s = (θ/360°)(2πr), which simplifies to s = (θ/180°)πr.
Worked Example

Find the arc length for a \( 120° \) sector of a circle with radius \( 4 \).

\( s = \dfrac{120°}{360°}(2\pi \cdot 4) = \dfrac{1}{3}(8\pi) = \dfrac{8\pi}{3} \)

faqs.question: How do I find arc length when the angle is given in radians?
faqs.answer:
Use the simplified formula s = rθ directly — multiply the radius by the angle measure in radians.
Worked Example

Find the arc length for a \( \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \) sector of a circle with radius \( 3 \).

\( s = r\theta = 3 \cdot \dfrac{5\pi}{6} = \dfrac{15\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{2} \)

faqs.question: How do I find the area of a sector when the angle is given in degrees?
faqs.answer:
Use the formula A = (θ/360°)(πr²) — the same "fraction of the whole" logic as arc length, just applied to the circle's full area instead of its full circumference.
Worked Example

Find the area of a \( 120° \) sector of a circle with radius \( 4 \).

\( A = \dfrac{120°}{360°}(\pi \cdot 4^2) = \dfrac{1}{3}(16\pi) = \dfrac{16\pi}{3} \)

faqs.question: How do I find the area of a sector when the angle is given in radians?
faqs.answer:
Use the simplified formula A = ½θr².
Worked Example

Find the area of a \( \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \) sector of a circle with radius \( 3 \).

\( A = \dfrac{1}{2}\theta r^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\cdot 3^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\cdot 9 = \dfrac{15\pi}{4} \)

faqs.question: What's the difference between arc length and sector area, and when do I use each formula?
faqs.answer: Arc length measures a curved DISTANCE (a 1-dimensional measurement, in units like inches or meters), while sector area measures a 2-dimensional REGION (in square units, like square inches). Use arc length when the question asks how far something travels along the curve itself; use sector area when the question asks how much surface or space the pie-slice-shaped region covers.

faqs.question: How does TR1 connect to what we're doing in TR2?
faqs.answer: TR2 leans directly on TR1's foundation. Standard position and the sign convention (positive counterclockwise, negative clockwise) from TR1 are exactly what let you find coterminal angles by rotating a full extra turn. And the radian definition from TR1 — an angle whose arc equals the radius — is precisely why the arc length formula simplifies so cleanly to s = rθ once you're working in radians.

faqs.question: Why do coterminal angles and arc length matter for the rest of the trig unit?
faqs.answer: Coterminal angles become essential once you start solving trig equations, since most equations have infinitely many solutions that are all coterminal with each other — you'll constantly be asked to find "all solutions" using the +k·360° idea from this section. Arc length and sector area also show up constantly in real-world applications of trig — anything involving wheels, gears, orbits, or circular motion relies on exactly this relationship between angle and distance.

guided.title: Practice Finding Coterminal Angles
guided.prompt: I'm learning to find coterminal angles. Give me an angle in degrees and ask me to find one larger and one smaller coterminal angle using the +k(360°) idea. Then give me an angle in radians and have me do the same thing using +k(2π). Check my work each time.

guided.title: Practice Finding the Principal Angle
guided.prompt: I'm learning to find the principal angle of a given angle. Give me a large angle (like over 720°) or a negative angle, and walk me through finding its principal angle step by step. Then give me a few more practice angles of increasing difficulty.

guided.title: Understand Where s = rθ Comes From
guided.prompt: I'm learning the arc length formula s = rθ for angles in radians. Can you help me understand why this formula makes sense, connecting it back to the definition of a radian as an angle that creates an arc equal to the radius? Then quiz me on a few arc length problems, mixing both degrees and radians.

guided.title: Practice Arc Length and Sector Area Together
guided.prompt: I'm learning both the arc length formula and the sector area formula. Give me a circle's radius and a central angle, and ask me to find both the arc length AND the sector area for that same sector. Check my work, and help me keep straight which formula uses r and which uses r².

guided.title: Connect Coterminal Angles to Solving Trig Equations
guided.prompt: I've learned about coterminal angles in TR2, and I've heard this becomes important later when solving trig equations. Can you explain, in a preview kind of way, why an equation like sin(θ) = 0.5 would end up having infinitely many solutions, and how coterminal angles explain that?

paths.label: TR2: Angle Position and Arc Length
paths.sectionLabel: TR2, Angle Position and Arc Length
paths.intro: Builds to the TR2 check: finding positive and negative coterminal angles, and finding the length of a circular arc.

stages.desc: Two quick skills TR2 leans on. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Convert less-common angles
stops.target: Convert between degrees and radians for angles like \(72^\circ\) or \(\dfrac{8\pi}{9}\), not just multiples of \(30^\circ\) and \(45^\circ\).
stops.solution: Multiply by pi/180: 72pi/180. Divide top and bottom by 36: 2pi/5.
stops.again: Convert \(280^\circ\) to radians, and \(\dfrac{8\pi}{9}\) to degrees.
stops.reflect: What is a good first factor to try when reducing a fraction over 180?

stops.title: Add and subtract 2π
stops.target: Add or subtract \(2\pi\) from a fraction of \(\pi\): first rewrite \(2\pi\) as a fraction with the same denominator, then combine the numerators.
stops.coldA:
Step 1: Write \(2\pi\) as a fraction over 5. \(2\pi = \dfrac{2\pi}{1} = \dfrac{2\pi \cdot 5}{1 \cdot 5} = \dfrac{10\pi}{5}\).
Step 2: Add. \(\dfrac{3\pi}{5} + \dfrac{10\pi}{5} = \dfrac{3\pi + 10\pi}{5} = \dfrac{13\pi}{5}\).
Step 3: Subtract. \(\dfrac{3\pi}{5} - \dfrac{10\pi}{5} = \dfrac{3\pi - 10\pi}{5} = -\dfrac{7\pi}{5}\).
stops.solution: Step 1: 2pi has no denominator, so write it as 2pi/1 and multiply the top and bottom by 5 to match: 2pi = 10pi/5. Step 2: now the denominators match, so add the numerators: 3pi/5 + 10pi/5 = 13pi/5. Step 3: subtract the numerators: 3pi/5 - 10pi/5 = -7pi/5.
stops.mistake: Adding 2 to the numerator (getting 5pi/5) instead of first rewriting 2pi as 10pi/5.
stops.reflect: What is the rule for rewriting \(2\pi\) over any denominator? (Hint: over 9, it is \(\dfrac{18\pi}{9}\).)

stages.desc: Coterminal angles first, then arc length, matching the two parts of the TR2 check.

stops.title: What coterminal means
stops.target: Coterminal angles share the same terminal side. They differ by a whole number of full turns: multiples of \(360^\circ\) or \(2\pi\).
stops.cold: Which of these are coterminal with \(30^\circ\)?   \(390^\circ\), \(-330^\circ\), \(330^\circ\)
stops.coldPlain: Which of these are coterminal with 30 degrees: 390, -330, 330 degrees?
stops.coldA:
Subtract each angle from \(30^\circ\) and ask: is the difference a full turn, \(360^\circ\) (or a multiple of it)?
\(390^\circ - 30^\circ = 360^\circ\): coterminal (one extra turn).
\(30^\circ - (-330^\circ) = 360^\circ\): coterminal (one turn backward).
\(330^\circ - 30^\circ = 300^\circ\): not coterminal. \(330^\circ\) ends in Quadrant IV.
stops.solution: Subtract each from 30 and see if the difference is a multiple of 360: 390 - 30 = 360 yes; 30 - (-330) = 360 yes; 330 - 30 = 300 no.
stops.mistake: Thinking -330 and 330 are both coterminal because they "look related."
stops.againA:
In radians a full turn is \(2\pi\). Over 4, that is \(2\pi = \dfrac{8\pi}{4}\).
\(\dfrac{11\pi}{4} - \dfrac{3\pi}{4} = \dfrac{8\pi}{4} = 2\pi\): coterminal.
\(\dfrac{3\pi}{4} - \left(-\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{8\pi}{4} = 2\pi\): coterminal.
\(\dfrac{3\pi}{4} - \left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{6\pi}{4}\): not a full turn, so not coterminal.
stops.reflect: How can you test whether two angles are coterminal?

stops.title: Coterminal angles in degrees
stops.target: Find a positive and a negative coterminal angle by adding and subtracting one full turn, \(360^\circ\).
stops.cold: Find one positive and one negative angle coterminal with \(144^\circ\).
stops.coldPlain: Find one positive and one negative angle coterminal with 144 degrees.
stops.coldA:
Why 360? One full turn is \(360^\circ\). Going around once more lands on the same terminal side.
Positive: add a full turn. \(144^\circ + 360^\circ = 504^\circ\).
Negative: subtract a full turn. \(144^\circ - 360^\circ = -216^\circ\).
stops.solution: Add 360 for a positive coterminal angle: 504 degrees. Subtract 360 for a negative one: -216 degrees. (Other answers, like 864 or -576, are also correct.)
stops.mistake: Subtracting 180, which gives the opposite direction instead of the same terminal side.
stops.again: Find a positive and a negative angle coterminal with \(40^\circ\).
stops.stretch: Find the angle between \(0^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\) coterminal with \(850^\circ\).
stops.stretchA:
\(850^\circ\) is more than two full turns, so subtract \(360^\circ\) until the angle is between \(0^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\):
\(850^\circ - 360^\circ = 490^\circ\) (still too big), then \(490^\circ - 360^\circ = 130^\circ\).
stops.reflect: Why is there more than one correct answer?

stops.title: Coterminal angles in radians
stops.target: Find coterminal angles in radians by adding and subtracting one full turn, \(2\pi\). First write \(2\pi\) as a fraction with the same denominator as the angle.
stops.cold: Find one positive and one negative angle coterminal with \(\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\).
stops.coldPlain: Find one positive and one negative angle coterminal with 2pi/5.
stops.coldA:
Step 1: Write \(2\pi\) over 5. \(2\pi = \dfrac{2\pi \cdot 5}{5} = \dfrac{10\pi}{5}\).
Step 2: Positive, add. \(\dfrac{2\pi}{5} + \dfrac{10\pi}{5} = \dfrac{12\pi}{5}\).
Step 3: Negative, subtract. \(\dfrac{2\pi}{5} - \dfrac{10\pi}{5} = -\dfrac{8\pi}{5}\).
stops.solution: Step 1: a full turn is 2pi. The angle has denominator 5, so rewrite 2pi as 2pi/1 = 10pi/5 (multiply top and bottom by 5). Step 2: add the numerators: 2pi/5 + 10pi/5 = 12pi/5. Step 3: subtract the numerators: 2pi/5 - 10pi/5 = -8pi/5.
stops.mistake: Skipping Step 1 and adding 2 to the numerator (getting 4pi/5), or adding 2pi/5 instead of 2pi.
stops.again: Find a positive and a negative angle coterminal with \(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\).
stops.stretch: Find the angle between \(0\) and \(2\pi\) coterminal with \(-\dfrac{17\pi}{4}\).
stops.stretchA:
Step 1: \(2\pi = \dfrac{8\pi}{4}\).
Step 2: the angle is negative, so add full turns until it is between 0 and \(2\pi\):
\(-\dfrac{17\pi}{4} + \dfrac{8\pi}{4} = -\dfrac{9\pi}{4}\), then \(-\dfrac{9\pi}{4} + \dfrac{8\pi}{4} = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), then \(-\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{8\pi}{4} = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\).
stops.reflect: How is this the same as adding \(360^\circ\) in degrees? What is the extra step in radians?

stops.title: Arc length with radians
stops.target: The length of an arc on a circle of radius \(r\) cut off by a central angle \(\theta\) in radians is \(s = r\theta\).
stops.cold: Find the length of the arc of a circle of radius 6 intercepted by an angle of \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\).
stops.coldPlain: Find the length of the arc of a circle of radius 6 intercepted by an angle of 5pi/6.
stops.solution: The angle is already in radians, so s = r * theta = 6 * 5pi/6 = 5pi.
stops.mistake: Using the formula with an angle in degrees.
stops.again: Radius 9, angle \(\dfrac{4\pi}{9}\). Find the arc length.
stops.reflect: Why does a bigger radius give a longer arc for the same angle?

stops.title: Arc length with degrees
stops.target: If the angle is in degrees, convert it to radians first, then use \(s = r\theta\).
stops.cold: Find the length of the arc of a circle of radius 10 intercepted by an angle of \(144^\circ\).
stops.coldPlain: Find the length of the arc of a circle of radius 10 intercepted by an angle of 144 degrees.
stops.mistake: Computing 10 * 144 = 1440, which uses degrees in a radian-only formula.
stops.again: Radius 12, angle \(40^\circ\). Find the arc length.
stops.reflect: What will you check for before using \(s = r\theta\) on the real check?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same two-part format as the TR2 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Find coterminal angles and an arc length, the way the TR2 check asks.
stops.cold:
(a) Find two angles, one positive and one negative, that are coterminal with \(\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\).
(b) Find the length of the arc of a circle of radius 5 intercepted by an angle of \(288^\circ\).
stops.coldPlain: (a) Find two angles, one positive and one negative, coterminal with 4pi/5. (b) Find the length of the arc of a circle of radius 5 intercepted by an angle of 288 degrees.
stops.coldA:
(a) Step 1: \(2\pi = \dfrac{2\pi \cdot 5}{5} = \dfrac{10\pi}{5}\). Step 2: \(\dfrac{4\pi}{5} + \dfrac{10\pi}{5} = \dfrac{14\pi}{5}\). Step 3: \(\dfrac{4\pi}{5} - \dfrac{10\pi}{5} = -\dfrac{6\pi}{5}\).
(b) Convert first: \(288^\circ \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \dfrac{8\pi}{5}\). Then \(s = 5 \cdot \dfrac{8\pi}{5} = 8\pi\).
stops.mistake: Forgetting to convert 288 degrees to radians before multiplying.
stops.again:
(a) Find a positive and a negative angle coterminal with \(160^\circ\).
(b) Find the arc length on a circle of radius 14 intercepted by an angle of \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\).
stops.againA:
(a) One full turn is \(360^\circ\): \(160^\circ + 360^\circ = 520^\circ\) and \(160^\circ - 360^\circ = -200^\circ\).
(b) Already in radians: \(s = 14 \cdot \dfrac{3\pi}{4} = \dfrac{42\pi}{4} = \dfrac{21\pi}{2}\).
stops.reflect: Which unit (degrees or radians) needs the extra step in each part?
